title: Luxury Safari Lodges in Kenya: 6 Exceptional Camps and How to Choose
meta_title: Luxury Safari Lodges in Kenya: 6 Exceptional Camps
meta_description: Luxury safari lodges in Kenya compared: 6 top camps in the Masai Mara, Laikipia and Lewa, what each suits and how to book. Advice from Nairobi.
excerpt: Our guide to luxury safari lodges in Kenya compares six exceptional camps in the Masai Mara, Laikipia and Lewa, with what each suits, costs to expect and booking tips.
content:
The best luxury safari lodges in Kenya are small, high-end tented camps and lodges in private conservancies and scenic edges of the big reserves, chiefly the Masai Mara, Laikipia and Lewa. Expect a handful of suites, private guides, flexible game drives, fine food and views, with fly-in access from Nairobi's Wilson Airport.

The hard part is choosing. Dozens of camps call themselves luxurious, and the photos all look alike. This guide from our Nairobi team explains where the top properties are, what each one suits, how luxury safari lodges in Kenya differ from standard lodges, and how to combine them into one smooth trip.

Photo by Meg von Haartman on Unsplash

Quick Facts

  • Best areas: Masai Mara conservancies, Mara Triangle edge, Laikipia, Lewa
  • Typical size: 7 to 30 tents or suites, far fewer than mainstream lodges
  • Best months: July to October for the migration; January to March for dry, quieter weather
  • Getting there: Scheduled light-aircraft flights from Wilson Airport, Nairobi, or by road
  • What is included: Usually full board and shared game drives; drinks, park or conservancy fees vary by camp
  • Book ahead: 9 to 12 months for July to October and Christmas

What Makes Luxury Safari Lodges in Kenya Different?

Luxury safari lodges in Kenya differ from standard lodges mainly in space and exclusivity, not just thread count. They have fewer rooms, more experienced guides, flexible schedules and usually sit in private conservancies where vehicle numbers are controlled, so sightings feel less crowded.

A standard safari lodge might have 60 to 100 rooms, set meal times and game drives on a fixed timetable. A luxury camp may have seven to fifteen tents, a guide who adjusts the day to the wildlife, and the option of walking, night drives or a bush breakfast that the national reserve rules do not allow everywhere.

Lodge or tented camp?

Most luxury safari lodges in Kenya are tented camps. The walls are canvas, but the rooms have proper beds, en-suite bathrooms with hot water, and private decks. Stone-and-glass lodges also exist, such as Angama Mara. The real difference is how close you feel to the bush, so choose by atmosphere, not by the word "lodge".

Reserve or conservancy?

The Masai Mara National Reserve is open to all vehicles, while the surrounding private conservancies are leased from Maasai landowners and limit beds and vehicles. Conservancy camps can usually offer walks and night drives. Our guide to the Masai Mara reserve versus its conservancies explains the trade-offs in detail.

Which Are the Best Luxury Safari Lodges in Kenya's Masai Mara?

The best luxury safari lodges in Kenya's Masai Mara sit either in the northern conservancies, such as Olare Motorogi, or on the escarpment above the Mara Triangle. Four stand out for very different reasons: Angama Mara for views, Mara Plains for intimacy, Mahali Mzuri for design and Cottar's 1920s Camp for old-style romance.

Photo: Divulge Adventures

Angama Mara (Oloololo Escarpment, Mara Triangle)

Angama Mara stands on the rim of the Oloololo Escarpment, which Angama Mara's own site describes as about 1,000 feet above the Mara plains. It has two separate camps of 15 tented suites each, all facing the view through glass fronts. A private road leads into the Mara Triangle, about ten minutes to the entrance, and balloon safaris, walks and photography sessions are offered.

Angama suits couples and photographers who want a dramatic setting and easy access to the Mara Triangle's river crossing points. Read our Mara Triangle guide for what this side of the ecosystem offers.

Mara Plains Camp (Olare Motorogi Conservancy)

Mara Plains Camp has only seven canvas suites raised on wooden decks in the Olare Motorogi Conservancy, on the northern boundary of the reserve. According to Great Plains Conservation's Mara Plains page, suites have copper baths, wood-burning stoves and over-bed air conditioning, and guests can borrow professional cameras and lenses. There is no fixed schedule, and game drives cover both the conservancy and the reserve.

Mahali Mzuri (Olare Motorogi Conservancy)

Mahali Mzuri is a camp of 12 luxury tents perched above a valley in the same conservancy. Virgin Limited Edition's Kenya page lists twice-daily game drives, a spa, walks with a Maasai guide and dawn balloon flights. Its bold tent design appeals to travellers who like contemporary style. For more on this area, see our Olare Motorogi Conservancy guide.

Cottar's 1920s Camp (southern Mara conservancy)

Cottar's 1920s Camp recreates a vintage safari style in a private conservancy on the southern side of the Mara. Cottar's own site lists eleven tents: five doubles, four family tents and two honeymoon tents. Guests can choose walks, e-bike outings, cultural visits, spa treatments and bush baths on their veranda, which makes it a strong pick for families and honeymooners.

Luxury Safari Lodges in Kenya Beyond the Mara: Laikipia and Lewa

Laikipia and Lewa, north of Mount Kenya, are the best places for luxury safari lodges in Kenya away from the Mara crowds. Conservancies here are large and private, with rhinos, Grevy's zebra, reticulated giraffe and activities such as horse riding, camel treks and walking that the national parks rarely allow.

Photo: Divulge Adventures

Loisaba Tented Camp (Loisaba Conservancy, Laikipia)

Loisaba Tented Camp sits in the 57,000-acre Loisaba Conservancy, on an important elephant movement corridor, according to Elewana's Loisaba Tented Camp page. Activities include day and night game drives, horse riding, camel treks, bush walks, mountain biking, fishing and visits to Samburu villages. It is ideal for active travellers and families who like variety.

Lewa Safari Camp (Lewa Wildlife Conservancy)

Lewa Safari Camp lies on the rolling plains of the 65,000-acre Lewa Wildlife Conservancy, north of Mount Kenya. Elewana's Lewa Safari Camp page describes large tented rooms with verandas and en-suite bathrooms, and wildlife that includes black and white rhinos, Grevy's zebra and more than 200 bird species. It is a good rhino stop on a northern Kenya circuit.

The region also has excellent options at Ol Pejeta, covered in our post on Ol Pejeta Safari Cottages, and in Samburu. Our Laikipia wilderness guide explains the area's conservancies, wildlife and access.

Amboseli and Tsavo also have high-end camps, usually on private land at the park edges, with views of Kilimanjaro in Amboseli. They work best as a second or third stop rather than the centrepiece of a luxury trip.

Photo: Divulge Adventures

How Much Does a Stay at Luxury Safari Lodges in Kenya Cost?

Luxury safari lodges in Kenya price per person per night, usually on a full-board basis with shared game drives included. Rates change with the season, so July to October and the festive season cost the most, while April, May and November are often far cheaper at the same camp.

When comparing quotes, check what each rate includes. Some camps include drinks, laundry, conservancy fees and airstrip transfers; others charge separately. Park and conservancy fees add a meaningful sum per day, which our Kenya park fees guide sets out. For a whole-trip budget, read our Kenya safari cost breakdown, and for Mara-specific options at every level see Masai Mara camps by budget.

Ways to keep the cost down

Travel in the shoulder months of June, early November or January to March, stay four or more nights at one camp, and mix one top-tier camp with a comfortable mid-range lodge. Many camps also offer family or stay-longer deals, and our team checks these for you when we build a quote.

How to Choose Luxury Safari Lodges in Kenya for Your Trip

Choose luxury safari lodges in Kenya by matching each camp to what you most want to see and do. Pick the Mara for big cats and the migration, Laikipia or Lewa for rhinos, walking and riding, and add Amboseli for elephants below Kilimanjaro. Two or three areas over seven to ten nights works well.

Photo: Divulge Adventures

How many nights should you stay at each camp?

Three nights per camp is the sweet spot. It gives you two full days, which matters in the Mara when you are waiting for a river crossing. One-night stops at luxury safari lodges in Kenya waste time on transfers and rarely let you settle into the camp's rhythm.

Should you fly or drive between luxury safari lodges in Kenya?

Flying suits shorter trips and remote northern conservancies, since light aircraft link Nairobi's Wilson Airport with airstrips near most camps. Bags on these flights are limited to soft bags with a low weight allowance, so read our Kenya safari packing list before you pack. Driving costs less and shows you the Rift Valley, but adds long road days. Our fly-in safari packages combine both.

Ready-made trips to start from

If you prefer a starting point, our 7-day luxury Mara river crossing safari covers Amboseli, Lake Nakuru and three nights in the Mara during migration season. Honeymooners should also read our Kenya honeymoon safari guide, and eco-minded travellers our post on eco lodges in the Masai Mara.

Insider Tips

  • Book the smallest camps first: Seven-suite camps such as Mara Plains fill early for July to October
  • Ask about the vehicle: Check whether game drives are shared or private, and what a private vehicle costs
  • Check inclusions: Compare drinks, laundry, conservancy fees and airstrip transfers, not just the nightly rate
  • Mix your styles: Pair one escarpment or design-led camp with one classic tented camp
  • Pack light: Light-aircraft flights take soft bags only, with strict weight limits
  • Balloon safaris: Book Mara balloon flights with your camp in advance; see our Masai Mara balloon safari guide

Frequently Asked Questions

Which area has the best luxury safari lodges in Kenya?

The Masai Mara has the widest choice of luxury safari lodges in Kenya, especially in the private conservancies on its northern edge, such as Olare Motorogi, where camps like Mara Plains and Mahali Mzuri limit guest numbers. Laikipia and Lewa are the best alternative for privacy, walking, horse riding and rhinos, and they pair well with a Mara stay.

Are luxury tented camps as comfortable as lodges?

Yes. Most luxury safari lodges in Kenya are actually tented camps, with canvas walls but proper beds, en-suite bathrooms, hot water and private decks. Mara Plains Camp, for example, has copper baths, wood-burning stoves and over-bed air conditioning. The canvas simply lets you hear the bush at night, which many guests see as part of the appeal.

How far ahead should I book a luxury safari lodge in Kenya?

Book luxury safari lodges in Kenya as early as you can for July to October, when the Great Migration is in the Masai Mara and the smallest camps fill first. Nine to twelve months ahead is sensible for those months and for Christmas. For January to March or the green season, a few months is often enough.

Can children stay at luxury safari lodges in Kenya?

Many luxury safari lodges in Kenya welcome children, but age rules vary by camp and by activity. Cottar's 1920s Camp, for instance, has four family tents, while some smaller camps set minimum ages for game drives or walks. Tell us your children's ages before we shortlist camps, so every suggestion fits your family.

How do you get to luxury safari lodges in Kenya?

Most travellers reach luxury safari lodges in Kenya on short scheduled light-aircraft flights from Nairobi's Wilson Airport to a bush airstrip near the camp, where the camp's guide meets them. Driving is also possible to the Mara, Laikipia and Amboseli, and it suits travellers who want to see more of the country on the way.

Final Thoughts

The finest luxury safari lodges in Kenya are small camps in the Mara conservancies, on the Oloololo Escarpment and across Laikipia and Lewa, each suited to a different kind of traveller. Combine two or three of them over a week or more, and book early for the migration months.
